questions.q: What is the specific failure mode this lesson describes for a network design that worked fine for three teams?
options: The design was always wrong, even at three teams
None of the individual decisions along the way were wrong for the team size at the time, but the design had no built-in answer for what happens as the number of teams grows
Azure and AWS impose a hard limit of three peered VNets or VPCs per hub
A hub-and-spoke topology cannot support more than ten spokes under any circumstance
questions.explain: Each decision was reasonable for the team count at the time; the problem is that nothing forced a revisit as the organization grew, so overlapping IP ranges and inconsistent access built up unnoticed.

questions.q: What is the single most common root cause of an expensive, unplanned network redesign according to this lesson?
options: Choosing AWS Transit Gateway instead of Azure Virtual WAN
Running too few spokes rather than too many
Using IaC modules instead of manually configuring each spoke
IP address overlap between two spokes that were each assigned the same CIDR block independently, with no central tracking
questions.explain: Two spokes independently assigned the same CIDR range, discovered only when they need to connect, forces an expensive re-addressing — the fix is a central address plan allocated before provisioning, not after.

questions.q: What does a standardized spoke template actually provide that ad hoc, manually built spokes do not?
options: It guarantees unlimited bandwidth on every ExpressRoute or Direct Connect circuit
It removes the need for any central IP address plan
It allows every spoke to set its own firewall policy independently of the hub
Every new spoke gets the correct CIDR, hub connectivity, routing, and DNS link applied consistently, with no chance of someone building the egress or DNS pattern slightly differently each time
questions.explain: A reusable IaC spoke module ensures every spoke is built the same way structurally, the same principle behind writing reusable modules generally — consistency survives past whoever built the first spoke.

questions.q: Why should per-spoke access through the hub default to "deny spoke-to-spoke" rather than allowing it broadly?
options: So that adding a new spoke never requires re-auditing every existing spoke, because each spoke's access stays scoped to only what it actually needs
Because Azure and AWS both prohibit any spoke-to-spoke traffic by policy
Because deny-by-default removes the need for a hub firewall entirely
Because hub-and-spoke only works if spokes can never reach shared services either
questions.explain: Scoping each spoke's access to what it actually needs — shared services, maybe one or two specific other spokes — keeps adding spoke thirty-one from requiring a re-audit of spokes one through thirty.

questions.q: How does this lesson draw the ownership boundary between a central network team and individual teams?
options: Individual teams own the hub's firewall policy; the central team owns nothing
Every decision, inside a spoke or at the hub, requires central team sign-off
The central team owns the hub, DNS zones, IP address plan, and spoke template; individual teams own what happens inside their own spoke
Neither the central team nor individual teams own anything — ownership is determined per incident
questions.explain: The central team owns what creates inconsistency or risk if duplicated per team (the hub, DNS, IP plan, spoke template); each team owns its own subnets, NSG rules, and application architecture inside its spoke.
